newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk banks expand networks despite narrow profits.
newsitem.headline: Turk banks expand networks despite narrow profits.

text.p: Turkey's private banks continue to expand their networks by opening new branches despite increased competition which boosts costs and squeezes profit margins.

Bankers said the race to open new branches, sparked by the 1994 financial crisis in a bid to draw cheaper domestic funds, is being perpetuated by the continued high cost of borrowing on international markets.
The emergence of new regional economic centres within the country is also encouraging branch expansion, they said.

"Turkish banks are aiming to give a wider range of services to their customers. It is obvious that the amount from the cake is falling as the number of bank branches increases," said Kemal Gurer, assistant general manager at medium-sized Esbank.
"But new economic centres are raising banks' appetite for new branches," he said.
Bankers warn that fierce competition among banks cut profits both because of rising costs and increased risks by expanding out to new customers.

"During the crisis banks closed some branches, but after the crisis they started expanding their bank branches for wider banking. But banks are due to come to an optimum level so they should be very careful while opening new branches," said Gulcin Esin, assistant general manager at small-sized Kentbank.

She said the bank was targeting to reach 50 branches by the end of this year, from 37 at the moment. The maximum number of new branches allowed in one year is limited to 10, but banks are allowed to carry over their allowance from the previous year, as Kentbank plans to do.
Turkey's current banking law requires banks to get Treasury approval to open a new branch after meeting financial ratio requirements.
Under a new banking law currently being drafted, the Treasury is expected to introduce further limitations on the opening of new branches.

But eastern and southeastern regions will be supported in line with an expected economic boom under the Southeast Anatolian Project (GAP) -- an ambitious network of irrigation and energy projects already boosting the region's economy.
The number of branches in Gaziantep, seen as the centre of the GAP region, rose by 11 to 76 in 1996.

"We are very happy with the business in Gaziantep as it has become a new economic centre in the region. We plan to open new branches in the southeast and eastern cities this year," Esbank's Gurer told Reuters.
Turkey's total bank branches numbered 6,442 in 1996, up from 6,241 in 1995.
Previously, the number had shrunk to 6,087 in 1994 from 6,212 a year earlier because of the closure of three small private banks in a liquidity shortage during the 1994 crisis.
Total bank deposits grew 25 percent in real terms in 1996, with state bank deposits leading the way with 27 percent real growth.
In Turkey there are 69 private and public commercial banks.

Technological developments in the banking sector are expected to lower demand for new bank branches as big banks start encouraging their customers to carry out transactions through electronic systems, bankers said.

Average deposits per branch rose to $7.1 million in 1995 from $5.1 million in 1991 according to figures from the Turkish Bankers' Association. Over the same period, total credits per branch climbed 18 percent to $4.7 million.
